items.passage: Eunseo had warned the passenger that the ferryman's house flooded every spring, but Anders followed her down to the cellar anyway, wading through cold water to help carry up her father's boxes. He had arrived in Tromso that morning with one suitcase and no plan, and he said so cheerfully, as if it were a credential. Lifting a crate of charts, Eunseo asked why anyone would choose a town this dark in winter. Anders did not answer at once. Instead he pointed to the waterline on the stone wall, then to the older lines above it, each one marked with a year in her father's hand. 'He kept starting over down here,' Anders said. 'Every spring, the same cellar.' Eunseo looked at the marks she had passed a thousand times and, for the first time, read them as a record of persistence rather than loss.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A conflict between two characters is introduced and then settled by a compromise.
A setting is described, followed by a flashback to the father's arrival in town.
A character's plan is explained, then abandoned after a setback in the cellar.
A shared task is shown, a question is raised, and a remark reframes the familiar.

items.passage: Paloma hated waiting rooms. She had tended the garden of the house on Calle Betis for thirty years, and she was used to hours that produced something: a pruned hedge, a bed of turned soil. Here in the hospital in Seville there was only the clock and Alba, the house's new owner, who had driven her in after the fall from the ladder. For a long time they spoke about nothing. Then Alba admitted that she had bought the house with money from a scholarship fund her late uncle had left, a fund meant for students who would now never receive it. She had wanted a garden more than she had wanted to be generous, she said. Paloma studied her bandaged wrist. 'Gardens cost too,' she said. 'Someone always pays for the shade.'
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It shows one character's impatience, presents another's confession, then a reflective reply.
It describes an accident in detail, then traces the injured character's recovery at home.
It compares two characters' careers before revealing they are rivals for the same house.
It recounts a dispute over money and ends with both characters agreeing to share the fund.

items.passage: Years later, I still think about the season Coach Sunethra benched me. I was the best bowler on our plantation cricket team outside Colombo, and I sulked on the boundary while she sent out girls who could barely grip the ball. Each evening after practice she walked the rows of tea with the pickers, carrying their baskets to the weighing shed, though no one paid her for it and the estate manager praised her only in speeches. I thought she was wasting her strength. One night I followed her, meaning to complain, and ended up carrying a basket myself. The pickers called me by my name, Nadeesha, as if they had always known it. Sunethra had benched me, I began to see, not to punish my arm but to show me where the team's real work happened.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a cricket match in detail, then explains why the team lost the final.
It recalls a grievance, describes a mentor's habit, then shows how joining it changed the writer.
It compares two coaching styles before arguing that the estate should pay its coaches.
It presents the pickers' complaints and then reports the estate manager's response.

items.passage: Wood remembers everything. Master Zihan said this whenever I, Shuang, rushed a joint in his workshop beside the abandoned orchard outside Chengdu, where his family had once grown pears. For two years I believed the orchard was simply forgotten, the trees left to split and grey because no one had time for them. Zihan's sons spoke of selling the land; his wife spoke of nothing at all. Then a furniture buyer from Shanghai came to see our tables. She walked past the polished samples, out to the orchard, and ran her hand along a fallen trunk. 'These are not neglected,' she said. 'He is drying them. This is twenty years of seasoning.' Zihan only nodded. I looked again at the rows and saw, for the first time, the careful spacing, the bark stripped in patient bands.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a carpenter's training methods, then lists the furniture a buyer purchased.
It recounts a family dispute over land and ends with the sons agreeing to sell it.
It presents a belief shared by the narrator and a family, then shows an outsider overturning it.
It contrasts two cities' craft traditions before describing the narrator's departure.

items.passage: Dakar was still asleep when the author Nneka and her translator, Babatunde, sat down at the bus stop on the hill road, where an old rule was painted on a board: Wait for the third bus; the first two belong to the goats. Nneka laughed and stood when the first bus came. Babatunde did not. 'In the story my village tells,' he said, 'a herder painted that rule after his goats were nearly crushed on this bend. The goats are gone, but he did not make the rule for goats alone.' Nneka sat back down, uncertain. The first bus passed, then the second, both crowded and swaying dangerously around the curve. When the third arrived, nearly empty, she climbed aboard, opened her notebook, and asked Babatunde how the herder's words should sound in her book.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A journey is planned, a delay occurs, and the characters abandon their trip entirely.
A legend is retold in full before the narrator explains its moral to the reader.
Two characters argue about a translation until one of them quits the project.
A rule is mocked, its origin is explained, and events lead a character to reconsider it.

items.passage: Minjun found the gift on the shared wall between their yards on Jeju Island: a jar of honey, labeled in Younghee's careful hand, tied with red string. He tasted it at once and winced. It was buckwheat honey, dark and bitter, the kind his own hives produced, the kind he had complained about to her all summer. Still, when Younghee peered over the wall that evening, he smacked his lips and praised its depth. __She beamed and confessed that she had traded three of her best jars for it, certain he had been hinting all along.__ Minjun kept smiling. The next morning he left a jar of his own buckwheat honey on the wall, labeled in his clumsiest hand, and waited to see whether she would pretend too.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals Younghee misread Minjun's complaints, raising the stakes of his pretense.
It shows that Younghee knew all along that Minjun disliked buckwheat honey.
It explains why Minjun decides to stop keeping bees on Jeju Island at last.
It introduces a rivalry between the neighbors over whose honey sells best.

items.passage: Ten slow laps in the salt-water pool off Kingston harbor: that was how my stepfather and I had always avoided talking. I was Janelle, nineteen, and he still called me 'the girl' to his friends, not unkindly. That morning we had to decide whether to move his mother, Kiara, out of the house in Port Royal where she had lived for sixty years and into our spare room. I expected him to insist; he was a man who liked decisions made. Instead, between laps, he floated on his back and told me how she had taught him to swim in this very pool, holding his chin above the water. __Then he asked what I thought she would want, and he waited for my answer.__ For the first time, I saw him not as my mother's husband but as a son afraid of choosing wrong.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows the stepfather testing the narrator before announcing a decision already made.
It explains why the family ultimately decides to keep Kiara in her house in Port Royal.
It marks a change in the stepfather's manner, showing he values the narrator's judgment.
It reveals the narrator's resentment at being asked to decide for the whole family.

items.passage: Noor was late again. She climbed the iron stairs to the projection booth above the old Beirut cinema two at a time, apologizing before the door had fully opened. Layla, who had threaded films in that booth for thirty years, did not look up from the reel. "The second reel sticks at the splice," she said. "Fix it." Noor fixed it in four minutes, a task that had once taken her most of an evening. __Layla merely grunted and turned to dust the lens, though she dusted the same corner of it for a long while.__ Later, when the audience below laughed at exactly the right moment, Layla remarked to no one in particular that the timing had been acceptable. Noor, already restless, was watching the street through the small square window, where the evening traffic had begun to thicken.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that Layla is displeased with how long Noor took to repair the reel.
It reveals that Layla cares more about the equipment than about Noor's work.
It introduces a conflict between Layla and Noor that the text later resolves.
It suggests that Layla is concealing her approval of Noor's improved skill.

items.passage: Who decides what an instrument is for? I, Remedios, asked myself this the winter I lodged at the monastery guesthouse in Gdansk, where a farmer named Katarzyna had come to claim her late uncle's brass theodolite. The monks had already promised it to me, the surveyor from the city, because the uncle's letter left it to "the one who measures." Katarzyna said she measured too: furrows, rainfall, the distance a cow wanders before dusk. The brothers smiled politely at this. __That night I watched her sight the bell tower through the eyepiece and call out its height to within a hand's breadth of my own figure.__ By morning the brothers had agreed that we should share the instrument, a season each, and that each of us should teach the other one thing. Snow had drifted against the guesthouse door, and we dug it out together before breakfast.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers evidence against the idea that only the narrator could rightly use the instrument.
It shows that Katarzyna cares more about the bell tower's height than about her uncle's gift.
It suggests that the narrator doubts the accuracy of her own earlier measurement of the tower.
It explains why the monks first promised the theodolite to the surveyor from the city.

items.passage: Ticking filled every room of our father's clock shop in Galicia, a hundred small hearts arguing over the exact time. Mateo and I had agreed to divide the house above it, but neither of us could say who would stay behind to keep the clocks wound. He spoke of the city as though it were already his address. I told myself I resented this, yet when I found he had quietly oiled the oldest pendulum before dawn, I could not hold on to my anger. Carmela, his wife, said he did it every morning and pretended he didn't. Slowly I began to see that my brother's restlessness was its own kind of loyalty, one that would rather leave than stand by and watch the shop fail. Outside, the rain kept the cobblestones dark until noon.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mateo?
options: Bitter resentment of Mateo's eagerness to abandon the family shop
Growing sympathy for motives that Mateo does not openly express
Quiet amusement at Mateo's attempts to hide his daily habits
Firm confidence that Mateo will ultimately choose to stay behind

items.passage: Three rules governed the salt barge that crossed the flats outside Kyoto: no fires below deck, no singing after dark, and no passengers who had not paid. Haruo had broken only the third. Captain Fumiko found him curled among the sacks on the second morning and, instead of putting him ashore, handed him a wool coat that had belonged to her late husband. He returned it the next day, folded with great care, without a word of thanks, and asked for work instead. A lesser boy would have kept both the coat and his silence; Haruo seemed to understand that a debt he could never repay would weigh on him more than the cold. He scraped salt from the rails until his palms cracked. Fumiko watched him, saying nothing, and hung the coat back on its nail beside the wheel.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Haruo's decision to return the coat?
options: Disapproval of Haruo's failure to thank the captain for her generosity
Confusion about why Haruo would refuse a gift he clearly needed
Respect for Haruo's wish to earn his place rather than owe it
Pity for Haruo's inability to accept kindness from a stranger

items.passage:
Baskets heavy with dark grapes swing from Giulietta's arms,
the Naples hillside bending in the heat behind her.
Daphne, her father's old friend, walks the terraces at noon
and tells the buyers whose hands first pruned these vines.
She does not mention the girl.
Giulietta hears, and lifts another basket.
What she grew she knows by touch:
the knot she tied in March, the cane she saved from frost,
the row she staked alone the week the rains came early.
Let the ledger carry Daphne's name in careful ink;
the vines lean, as they always have, toward the one who stays.
At dusk a cart rattles down the road,
and swallows stitch the sky above the press.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Giulietta?
options: Frustration that Giulietta will not insist on credit from the buyers
Concern that Giulietta's labor will soon be forgotten by everyone
Amusement at Giulietta's stubborn refusal to stop working at noon
Admiration for Giulietta's steady confidence in the work she has done

items.passage: Four buses, two transfers, forty minutes each way: that was the price of every lesson with Tommaso, and I paid it for six years. When he sold his house in Bologna, he asked me to meet him at the bus depot with the last thing he had not given away, a music stand so battered it leaned to the left. He had corrected my bowing beside that stand a thousand times, and he had rarely praised me. "Take it," he said, "and fix your posture." I used to think his strictness was coldness. Standing among the idling engines, I saw that he had saved this one object for me, and I began to understand that his corrections had been a way of paying attention. My bus arrived late, its windows fogged with the breath of strangers.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Tommaso?
options: Fond appreciation for a teacher whose severity reflected genuine care
Lingering resentment of a teacher who rarely offered any praise at all
Mild indifference toward a teacher she no longer expects to see again
Anxious uncertainty about whether she ever truly pleased her teacher

items.passage: Years later, I still remember the morning the ferry was cancelled and I waited out the rain under a fruit stall at the Auckland market. I was nineteen and furious, because my teacher had told me the day before that my essays were "tidy and empty." A stranger named Makana sheltered beside me, peeling a feijoa with his thumb. When I repeated the remark, expecting outrage on my behalf, he only asked my name. "Kian," he said, trying it out, "what would you write if nobody graded it?" I answered with a long speech about fairness, and I wince, fondly, at how certain I sounded. That boy believed a teacher's judgment was an injury rather than a door. The rain eased by eleven, and the vendors began stacking crates of kumara along the curb.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward his younger self?
options: Harsh disapproval of the anger he once directed at his teacher
Affectionate amusement at the confidence he once had in his complaint
Deep regret that he ignored the advice the stranger offered him
Nostalgic longing for the certainty he felt about fairness as a boy

items.passage:
I owe you an answer, Kainoa. You asked me on the stone bridge last week why I keep the shave-ice stand open when it loses money every winter, and I gave you a joke instead. You deserved better than that. Your doubts are not disloyalty; your father had the same sharp eye for numbers, and I trusted it then. You were right that the ledger looks grim. Still, I want you to sit with me and go through it, line by line, before either of us decides anything. If the numbers say close, I will listen, and I would rather hear that from you than from a bank. The stream under the bridge has been loud with rain since Tuesday, and the mango tree behind the stand is finally fruiting.
With love,
Caoimhe
items.question: Which choice best describes Caoimhe's attitude toward Kainoa's doubts about the business?
options: Irritation that Kainoa questions decisions his father made long ago
Amusement at Kainoa's habit of worrying too much about money
Respect for Kainoa's judgment as worth weighing seriously with her
Determination to prove Kainoa wrong by keeping the stand open

items.passage: We ate in two shifts at the summer camp in Manila, and Lan, the cook, always served his nephew Leilani last. Years earlier Leilani had borrowed money from him for a bus ticket home and never repaid it, and the campers knew only that the two did not speak. On the final night Leilani waited until the hall emptied, set an envelope beside the rice pot, and said he was sorry it had taken so long. Lan pushed the envelope back. He had kept count of the silence, he said, not the pesos, and no apology could buy back the summers they had spent avoiding each other's eyes. Still, he filled a second plate and set it across from his own. Outside, the generator coughed, and moths gathered thick around the bulb above the door.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Leilani finally repays his uncle on the camp's last night after years of avoiding him.
Lan's careful way of serving meals reveals how strictly the camp kitchen is run.
Honesty about borrowed money is always the surest way to keep a family's trust.
Lan mourns the lost closeness more than the money, yet begins to let his nephew in.

items.passage: "You're mapping the wrong thing," Aaliyah said, before I had even unfolded my tablet. She had swept the Garfield platform for twenty years, and she watched me photograph the stairwells as though I were counting someone's teeth. I was a surveyor for the transit authority, sent to recommend which entrances to close. She walked me down to the street and pointed out the corner store that kept its lights on for kids after late practice, and the bench where Jamal from the barbershop waited for his mother's train. "People don't take the shortest way," she told me. "They take the way that's watched." That evening I redrew two of my lines. A freight train groaned past on the far tracks, its cars rusted the color of dried leaves.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator learns that residents' routes depend on community care more than on efficiency.
Aaliyah distrusts the surveyor because she worries the station changes will cost her the job.
The narrator documents the station's stairwells to explain why some entrances must close.
Familiar places always matter more to people than any new development possibly could.

When the storm drained out of the stairwell, it left a tin box wedged beneath the cracked third step.
ODILE: (kneeling) My mother hid things. I told you so on the first day, and you translated it as "my mother was careful."
GENEVIEVE: The lawyer only needed the facts.
ODILE: (opening the box; letters inside) These are the facts. Read them to me in the words she used, not the polite ones.
GENEVIEVE: (hesitates, then reads slowly) "I am not sorry I stayed."
(ODILE sits down on the wet step.)
ODILE: All those meetings, you made her sound smaller than she was.
GENEVIEVE: (quietly) I'll do it properly this time.
(Below, a door slams, and rainwater ticks steadily from the banister onto the tiles.)
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how a storm damaged a staircase and exposed a hidden box of letters
To show a client pressing her interpreter to convey her mother's words faithfully
To explain the legal process by which Odile's family property must be settled
To suggest that the past always returns to those who try to hide from it

### lit40-medium-03-020 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 underlined_portion_function · 요청 난이도 medium

Ten slow laps in the salt-water pool off Kingston harbor: that was how my stepfather and I had always avoided talking. I was Janelle, nineteen, and he still called me 'the girl' to his friends, not unkindly. That morning we had to decide whether to move his mother, Kiara, out of the house in Port Royal where she had lived for sixty years and into our spare room. I expected him to insist; he was a man who liked decisions made. Instead, between laps, he floated on his back and told me how she had taught him to swim in this very pool, holding his chin above the water. __Then he asked what I thought she would want, and he waited for my answer.__ For the first time, I saw him not as my mother's husband but as a son afraid of choosing wrong.

### lit40-medium-03-022 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 underlined_portion_function · 요청 난이도 medium

Ticking filled every room of our father's clock shop in Galicia, a hundred small hearts arguing over the exact time. Mateo and I had agreed to divide the house above it, but neither of us could say who would stay behind to keep the clocks wound. He spoke of the city as though it were already his address. I told myself I resented this, yet when I found he had quietly oiled the oldest pendulum before dawn, I could not hold on to my anger. Carmela, his wife, said he did it every morning and pretended he didn't. Outside, the rain kept the cobblestones dark until noon.

the Naples hillside bending in the heat behind her.
Daphne, her father's old friend, walks the terraces at noon
and tells the buyers whose hands first pruned these vines.
She does not mention the girl.
Giulietta hears, and lifts another basket.

the knot she tied in March, the cane she saved from frost,
the row she staked alone the week the rains came early.

At dusk a cart rattles down the road,
and swallows stitch the sky above the press.

### lit40-medium-03-029 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 main_idea_or_purpose · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 곳의 근거를 합쳐 요지를 잡아야 하고, 오답 하나는 일화 요약에 그치는 부분 요지다
